story.title: Juno and the Buzzy Bee Hive
story.subtitle: A tiny trip inside a very busy hive.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Egg
chapters.text:
Juno sat on her bedroom floor. Her favorite toy was a toy triceratops. It had one amber eye. Amber is old tree sap. It turned hard, like candy.

Tonight that eye glowed gold. It went BZZZZZ! A tiny bee popped right out. "Hello, Juno. I'm Pip!" She waved her see-through wings. "Want to visit my hive?"

"Yes, yes, YES!" said Juno. The amber eye opened like a window. WHOOSH! Juno shrank down tiny. She zoomed inside, right behind Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: So Many Bees!
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, bees buzzed everywhere. Up, down, all around!

"This is my family," said Pip. "We have one queen. We have lots and lots of worker bees. They are all girls!"

"How many is lots?" asked Juno. She started counting. "One, two, three..."

Pip giggled. "Keep going. You'll be counting all night!" There were so many bees, nobody could count them all.

Juno laughed and gave up counting. "That's a whole lot of buzzing cousins!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Busy Queen
chapters.text:
A big bee walked by, slow and round. "That's our queen," said Pip. "She is the mommy of the whole hive."

"What does she do all day?" Juno asked.

"She lays eggs," said Pip. "Guess how many, in one day?"

Juno thought hard. "Five?"

"Try two thousand!" said Pip.

Juno's mouth popped open. "TWO THOUSAND baby bees, every single day?!"

"Yup," said Pip. "She's the busiest mom around."

Juno clapped her hands. "Go, Queen, go!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Every Job There Is
chapters.text:
"What do the other bees do?" Juno asked.

"Everything!" said Pip. "Worker bees clean the hive. They guard the door. They fly out for flowers. Every bee takes turns at every job."

"Can I try a job?" Juno asked.

"Be our guard," said Pip.

Juno stood by the tiny door. BUZZ! A bee zoomed home, carrying something yellow and sweet. Juno opened the door wide. "Welcome home!" she said.

The tired bee zipped past, happy and full.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
One bee wiggled in circles, shaking her whole body.

"Why is she dancing?" Juno giggled.

"That's not just dancing," said Pip. "It's a secret map! Her wiggles tell everyone where the best flowers are."

"No way!" said Juno.

"A long time ago, a scientist named Karl watched bees do this. He figured out their wiggly secret."

Juno tried it herself. She wiggled and waggled across the floor. The bees buzzed around her, delighted.

"Am I doing it right?" Juno asked.

"Close enough!" laughed Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Five Little Eyes
chapters.text:
Pip landed on Juno's hand. "Look closely," she said. "How many eyes do I have?"

Juno peeked. "Two big ones!"

"Keep looking," said Pip.

Juno squinted. "Wait... three tiny ones on top!"

"Five eyes, all together!" said Pip. "The big ones see shapes and colors. The tiny ones just feel the light."

Juno counted on her fingers. "One, two, three, four, FIVE! You win the eye contest, Pip."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Buzziest Wings
chapters.text:
"Why do you buzz?" asked Juno, covering her ears a little.

"My wings flap super fast," said Pip. "So fast your eyes can't even see them move!"

"Can I buzz too?" Juno flapped her arms as fast as she could. FLAP FLAP FLAP!

"Nothing happened," she panted.

Pip laughed. "My wings flap two hundred times every second. Way faster than arms!"

Juno flopped down giggling. "No wonder you sound like a tiny motorcycle!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Six Sunny Sides
chapters.text:
Pip led Juno to the honeycomb, rows of little rooms made of wax.

"Why are they shaped like that?" Juno asked, touching one. Each room had six straight sides.

"Six sides hold the most honey," said Pip, "using the least wax. Bees are great builders!"

"Can I help build one?" Juno asked. She lined up six pretend blocks in a circle. CLICK! They fit together perfectly, just like the real comb.

"You're a honeycomb champion!" cheered Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Honey Forever
chapters.text:
"One bee makes only a tiny drop of honey her whole life," said Pip. "But all my sisters together visit millions of flowers, just to fill one little jar."

Juno dipped her finger in honey. "Mmm, worth it!"

"Honey never goes bad," added Pip. "Even honey from ancient Egypt still tastes sweet today."

"And bees," Pip smiled, "buzzed around back when dinosaurs stomped the earth. Some got stuck in amber, just like your toy's eye."

Juno gasped. "My triceratops has a REAL bee friend inside!"

The amber glowed again. WHOOSH! Juno landed softly on her bedroom floor, a tiny drop of honey glistening on her fingertip.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Bee happy, and sleep tight, little buzzer.

true_facts.text: A bee family has one queen and lots and lots of worker bees, who are all girls.
The queen bee lays about **two thousand** eggs every single day.
Worker bees take turns doing every job — cleaning, guarding the door, and flying out for flowers.
Bees do a **wiggle dance** to show their sisters where the best flowers are.
A bee has **five eyes** — two big ones and three tiny ones on top.
A bee's wings flap **two hundred times** every second — that's the buzzing sound!
Honeycomb rooms have **six sides** because that shape holds the most honey using the least wax.
One bee makes only a tiny drop of honey in her whole life.
All the bees together visit millions of flowers just to fill one little jar of honey.
Honey never goes bad — honey from **ancient Egypt** still tastes sweet today.
Bees were buzzing around even when dinosaurs stomped the earth, long, long ago.

new_recurring.rule: The amber eye on Juno's toy triceratops glows gold and buzzes when a new adventure begins, opening a tiny window she can shrink through and explore, always returning her safely home at the end.

fact_pack.summary: Bees are flying insects living almost everywhere flowers grow, and a honeybee hive works together like one giant family. Beyond making honey, bees pollinate much of the food people eat, and scientists still study how these tiny insects talk and find their way home.

facts.text: A honeybee colony usually has one queen, tens of thousands of female worker bees, and a smaller number of male drones.
A healthy queen bee can lay up to about 2,000 eggs a day during the busy spring season.
Worker bees are all female and take turns doing every job in the hive, from cleaning cells to guarding the entrance to flying out to find flowers.
A drone's only job is to mate with a queen, and hives push drones out before winter because they cannot forage or sting to help defend the colony.
Scientists have described roughly 20,000 species of bees around the world, and only a few of them, like the honeybee, make the honey people eat.
Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch discovered that honeybees perform a 'waggle dance' to tell each other a flower's direction and distance.
Karl von Frisch won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973 for figuring out how bees communicate through dance and scent.
One worker honeybee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire lifetime.
Bees in a colony together may visit roughly two million flowers to gather enough nectar to make just one pound of honey.
Because honey has very little water and is naturally acidic, sealed pots of honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs are still edible thousands of years later.
A bee has five eyes in total: two large compound eyes for seeing shapes and colors, plus three tiny simple eyes on top of its head for sensing light.
A honeybee's wings beat about 200 times every second, and that fast flapping is what makes the buzzing sound people hear.
Only female bees have a stinger, and a honeybee worker's stinger is barbed so it stays in mammal skin, which means she dies soon after she stings.
Bees and other pollinators help produce roughly one out of every three bites of food humans eat, including apples, blueberries, and almonds.
Each spring, truckloads of honeybee hives are shipped into California to pollinate its almond orchards.
Beekeepers began widely reporting Colony Collapse Disorder in 2006, when many adult worker bees mysteriously left their hives and did not return.
Researchers link colony losses to several causes together: mites, disease, pesticides, and lost flowering habitat.
Honeycomb cells are built in a six-sided hexagon shape because it lets bees store the most honey while using the least amount of wax.
On cold days bees cluster and shiver their flight muscles to keep the hive near 95°F (35°C).
Bees preserved in amber roughly 100 million years old show bees lived alongside dinosaurs.
Egyptian wall art from around 2400 BC shows beekeepers collecting honeycomb, among the oldest farming records.
A single honeybee hive can hold 20,000 to 80,000 bees at the height of summer.

timeline.event: Bees appear in the fossil record, preserved in amber
Egyptian art shows people keeping bees and collecting honey
Karl von Frisch wins the Nobel Prize for decoding the bee waggle dance
Colony Collapse Disorder is first widely reported in the United States

story.title: Omar and the Bell That Remembered Bikes
story.subtitle: A rolling, rattling, flying-machine kind of night

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Bell in the Garage
chapters.text:
Omar stood in his driveway under the porch light. His BMX bike leaned against the fence, scuffed and ready. He had just landed his best bunny hop ever, clearing the rake in the grass. "Did you see that?" he whispered, grinning.

Inside the garage, something on the shelf began to glow. A small brass bell, dusty and forgotten, pulsed soft gold. Omar crept closer and picked it up. It rang all by itself. **DING!**

"About time," said a tiny voice. The bell had a round, cheerful face now. "I'm Spoke," it said. "Want to see where your bike came from?"

Before Omar could answer, the garage door swirled like water. He stepped through and landed in soft mud, beside a strange wooden machine with two wheels and no pedals at all.

"This is **1817**," Spoke said. "A German inventor named **Karl von Drais** built this. He called it the running machine."

"Where are the pedals?" Omar asked.

"There aren't any," Spoke said. "You push it along with your feet, like walking, only faster."

Omar hopped on, planted his sneakers, and pushed. **WHOOSH!** The wheels rolled smooth and steady. "It steers just like mine!" he shouted, swinging the handlebars side to side.

Spoke chuckled. "People called it the hobby horse. Looks like you just tamed it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker Road
chapters.text:
The ground rumbled under new wheels before Omar even sat down.

"Welcome to the **1860s**," Spoke said. "French builders **Pierre Michaux** and **Pierre Lallement** bolted pedals straight onto the front wheel."

Omar climbed on. The cobblestone street shook the whole bike. **RATTLE RATTLE RATTLE!**

"Why does it feel like my teeth are falling out?" Omar laughed.

"That's why people called it the boneshaker," Spoke said. "Hard wheels plus bumpy roads equals one wobbly ride."

Omar pedaled hard, bouncing over every stone, grinning the whole way. "Worst ride ever," he said, "but kind of awesome."

"Lallement even got a patent for this pedal idea, in the United States, in **1866**," Spoke added. A patent, Spoke explained, is like a paper that says an idea belongs to you.

Omar rubbed his sore elbow and laughed again. "Next bike better be smoother."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Wheel
chapters.text:
A shadow rolled past, tall as a doorway. Omar's jaw dropped.

"That," said Spoke, "is a **penny-farthing**, from the **1870s**. Named after two old coins — one huge, one tiny — just like its wheels."

The front wheel towered over Omar's head. A rider pedaled by, perched way up high.

"Isn't that dangerous?" Omar asked, watching the rider wobble over a bump.

"Sometimes," Spoke admitted. "If the front wheel stopped suddenly, the rider could tip right over the handlebars. They called that taking a header."

The wobbly rider caught his balance just in time and rolled on, laughing. Omar let out a breath. "Phew. Glad he's okay."

"Riders loved the speed," Spoke said. "One pedal turn and that giant wheel just flies. But somebody was bound to build something safer."

"Good," Omar said. "Let's go find them."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Starley's Safety Trick
chapters.text:
A workshop buzzed with hammers. Omar spotted a bike with two wheels the same size.

"**1885**," Spoke said. "**John Kemp Starley** built this. He called it the Safety Bicycle."

Omar crouched down and found a metal loop connecting the pedals to the back wheel. "Wait — that's a chain! Just like mine!"

"Exactly," Spoke said. "The chain turns the back wheel, so both wheels can stay low and even."

Omar hopped on and pedaled around the workshop. No towering wheel, no scary wobble. "This feels normal," he said. "This feels like a *bike* bike."

"That's the idea," Spoke said. "Lower, steadier, way easier to ride. Pretty soon, everybody wanted one."
chapters.shout_line: THAT'S A CHAIN! JUST LIKE MINE!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Bumpy Tire Problem
chapters.text:
Omar rolled the safety bicycle over a rock and felt every bump in his spine.

"Ouch," he said. "These tires are hard as rocks."

"They basically are rocks — solid rubber," Spoke said. "**1888**. Over in Scotland, a man named **John Boyd Dunlop** had the exact same complaint."

"What did he do?" Omar asked.

"He wrapped a rubber tube around the wheel and filled it with air," Spoke said, "like blowing up a balloon."

Omar grinned. "That's basically what's inside my BMX tires!"

"Exactly the idea," Spoke said. "Dunlop built it for his son's tricycle first. Smoother rides for everybody after that." Dunlop's company, Spoke added, still makes tires today.

Omar bounced the air-filled wheel and felt it cushion every rock. "Way better," he said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Everyone Gets Rolling
chapters.text:
Streets full of bikes stretched in every direction. Bells rang everywhere. **DING DING DING!**

"The **1890s**," Spoke said. "People called it the Golden Age. Millions of bikes, sold everywhere."

Omar noticed something. Most riders were men. A few women pedaled by in long, swishy skirts, fighting to keep the fabric from catching in the wheels.

"Their skirts keep getting stuck," Omar said. "They need different clothes."

"Good eye," Spoke said. "That's exactly what happened. Women started wearing baggy pants called bloomers instead, so they could pedal safely."

"A famous woman named **Susan B. Anthony** said bikes gave women more freedom to go places on their own than almost anything else," Spoke said.

Omar watched a woman in bloomers zoom past, laughing. "Good for her," he said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop That Learned to Fly
chapters.text:
A small shop sign read Wright Cycle Co. Omar peeked inside at shelves of spoked wheels and thin metal tubes.

"**Dayton, Ohio**, **1890s**," Spoke said. "Brothers **Wilbur and Orville Wright** ran this bike shop."

Omar picked up a light metal tube. "This is so light. Could this fly?"

Spoke smiled. "Good question. They thought so too."

"They used what they learned building light bike frames and wheels," Spoke said, "to help build something new. An airplane."

"In **1903**," Spoke added, "it actually flew."

Omar set the tube down carefully, eyes wide. "From bike shop... to the sky."

"Pretty great plot twist," Spoke said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Driveway
chapters.text:
The garage door swirled again. Omar landed back on his own driveway, bike still leaning on the fence.

"One more thing," Spoke said. "Gear shifters called derailleurs showed up in the **1930s**, so riders could switch gears on hills. And back in **1903**, racers started the Tour de France, a race across France that's still run today."

"And BMX bikes?" Omar asked, patting his handlebars.

"Those showed up in the **1970s**," Spoke said, "built small and tough for tricks, just like yours."

Omar grinned. "Best chapter yet."

"Today there are more than a billion bikes in the world," Spoke said. "More than any other ride on wheels."

Omar set the bell back on the shelf. It gave one last soft **DING** and dimmed to brass.

He climbed into bed, already dreaming of his next trick.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Pedal on, and dream well.

fact_pack.summary: Bicycles evolved over 200 years from a wooden walking machine with no pedals to today's lightweight, geared bikes ridden by billions of people. Along the way inventors added pedals, chains, air-filled tires, and gears, making bikes faster, safer, and more comfortable.

facts.text: In 1817, German inventor Karl von Drais built the 'Laufmaschine' or 'running machine,' a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals that riders pushed along with their feet.
Von Drais's invention was nicknamed the 'draisine' or 'hobby horse' and was steered with handlebars, much like a modern bike.

In the 1860s, French makers Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement added pedals directly to the front wheel, creating the 'velocipede,' nicknamed the 'boneshaker' for its rough ride on cobblestone streets.
Pierre Lallement patented a pedal-driven bicycle design in the United States in 1866.
In the 1870s, the 'penny-farthing' bicycle appeared, with a giant front wheel (sometimes taller than a person) and a tiny back wheel, letting riders go faster with one pedal turn.
Penny-farthings were named after two British coins of very different sizes, the large penny and the small farthing.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky because the rider sat high above the front wheel and could be thrown headfirst in a sudden stop, a fall nicknamed 'taking a header.'
In 1885, Englishman John Kemp Starley invented the 'Rover Safety Bicycle,' with two similarly sized wheels and a chain driving the back wheel, much closer to modern bikes.
The safety bicycle's lower, even wheels made it much easier and safer to ride than the penny-farthing, and it quickly became the standard design worldwide.
In 1888, Scottish inventor John Boyd Dunlop developed the practical pneumatic (air-filled) rubber tire, making bike rides much smoother than solid rubber tires.
Dunlop's tire company grew into the Dunlop Tyre brand, still famous today for tires on bikes and cars.
The 1890s bicycle craze, called the 'Golden Age of Bicycles,' saw millions of bikes sold across Europe and the United States.
Bicycles gave women new freedom to travel independently in the 1890s, and American reformer Susan B. Anthony said cycling 'has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world.'
Because long skirts were dangerous around bike gears and wheels, the bicycle craze helped popularize more practical clothing for women, including bloomers.
Wilbur and Orville Wright, who later invented the first successful airplane in 1903, ran a bicycle repair and manufacturing shop in Dayton, Ohio in the 1890s.
The Wright brothers used bicycle-building skills, like lightweight metal tubing and spoked wheels, to help design their early flying machines.
Multi-speed gear systems, called derailleurs, became common on bikes in the 1930s, letting riders shift gears to handle hills more easily.
The Tour de France, the world's most famous long-distance cycling race, began in 1903 and today covers about 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) across France over about three weeks.
BMX bikes, small and sturdy for tricks and dirt racing, became popular in the United States in the 1970s, inspired by motocross motorcycles.
Mountain bikes with wide, knobby tires were developed in the 1970s in Marin County, California, by riders who wanted to bike down rough dirt trails.
Today, an estimated one billion or more bicycles exist worldwide, more than any other kind of vehicle.
The Netherlands and Denmark are famous today for having more bicycles than cars in some cities, with wide bike lanes built for everyday cyclists.
Modern bicycles are made from lightweight materials like aluminum and carbon fiber, letting racing bikes weigh less than 8 kilograms (about 17 pounds).

story.title: Sam and the Wall-Walking Gecko
story.subtitle: A very sticky, very silly bedtime climb

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gecko on the Shelf
chapters.text:
Sam sat on the back porch with his bug jar. Inside sat one roly-poly and a whole lot of dirt. A ladybug had gotten away. A spider had waved one leg and scooted under a leaf.

Sam loved bugs. Spiders were his favorite. Geckos were his favorite too. He picked up every bug he found, gentle hands, soft catch, quick look, and then let it go again. That was the rule.

The sun was going down. It was almost bedtime.

Inside his room, a toy gecko sat on the shelf. His name was Tokay. Sam had never once noticed that his eyes could glow.

Tonight, they did. Green. Bright. Blinking like a tiny stoplight.

"Psst," said a small voice. "Sam. Over here."

Sam froze. The gecko on the shelf was talking.

"I'm Tokay," said the gecko. He hopped off the shelf onto Sam's pillow. He was warm now, like a real lizard, not a toy one anymore. "Want to see how I climb walls?"

Sam's mouth fell open. "Walls? You're not even outside!"

"Watch," said Tokay.

He scampered straight up the wall. Up, up, up, over the window, onto the ceiling. He hung there, upside down, grinning like it was the easiest thing in the world.

"WHOA!" shouted Sam.

"My toes have a trick," said Tokay. "Millions of tiny hairs called **setae**. Like a zillion itty-bitty eyelashes on each toe. They grab onto bumps too small for your eyes to see."

Sam looked at his own fingers. No tiny hairs there. "Can I have some?"

"Better," said Tokay. "Climb with me instead."

He tapped the wall twice. A little green door opened, right where the paint used to be. Through it, Sam could see grass, leaves, and a whole lot of climbing creatures waiting.

Sam grabbed his bug jar, just in case, and stepped through.

CLICK. The door shut softly behind them both.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Spider on the Window
chapters.text:
On the other side of the door was Sam's own garden. But everything looked bigger. Or maybe Sam was smaller. The grass blades towered over him like little green trees.

A thread of silk swung past his nose. At the end of it hung a spider, swaying gently in the night breeze.

"A spider!" Sam grinned. Spiders were his favorite thing in the whole wide world.

The spider climbed straight up the window glass. No ladder. No rope. Just up, step by careful step.

"How does she do that?" Sam asked.

"Look close," said Tokay. "Spiders have tiny hairs too. Thousands of them, on every foot. We call them setules, just a spider's own kind of sticky toe-hairs."

Sam pressed his nose near the glass, careful not to touch. The spider's feet looked fuzzy, almost like tiny little brushes.

"She's not using glue," said Tokay. "Just hugging the glass with her hairy feet."

Sam counted the spider's legs out loud. "One, two, three... eight!"

"Good counting," said Tokay.

The spider reached the top of the window and waved one leg, like a hello.

Sam waved back. "Hi, spider friend. You're really good at that."

"Ready for the next stop?" asked Tokay.

"Yes!" said Sam, bouncing on his toes. "Where to next?"

Tokay pointed up, toward a buzzing sound near the porch light, loud and busy.

"Follow the buzz," he said.

The two of them scrambled up the window frame together, Sam's sneakers somehow sticking just a little, just enough to help him along.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Buzzy Fly
chapters.text:
The buzzing got louder. A fat fly landed on the porch light, right side up, then flipped upside down without falling off even once.

"Whoa, how?" said Sam.

"Flies have tiny pads on their feet," said Tokay. "Each pad lets out a tiny drop of sticky juice. Like one little dab of honey on every foot."

Sam leaned close. "Sticky juice feet. That's silly."

"Silly and smart," said Tokay. "The juice glues the fly down for just a second. Then it unsticks and steps again."

The fly buzzed in a circle, landed on the porch ceiling, and sat there like nothing in the world was strange.

Sam reached toward his jar, then stopped. He remembered his own rule. Watch, don't grab.

"I won't catch her," Sam said. "I just want to watch."

"Good climber's rule," said Tokay, nodding his gecko head proudly. "Look close. Hands off."

A shiny round beetle thumped down next to the fly with a tiny bonk.

"Beetles use the same trick," said Tokay. "Sticky little footprints, everywhere they walk."

Sam giggled so hard he snorted. "Footprints made of glue juice. That's the silliest thing I ever heard in my whole life."

"Wait until you hear about ants," said Tokay, grinning, and he scuttled off the porch light toward a crack in the sidewalk, Sam hurrying right behind him.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Ant Parade
chapters.text:
A whole line of ants marched up the garden wall, carrying crumbs bigger than themselves.

"Up a wall? With crumbs?" Sam said. "That looks really hard."

"Ants carry two tools," said Tokay. "Sharp little claws for rough walls, sticky pads for smooth ones. They just pick whichever tool fits the job."

Sam watched one ant switch from rough brick to a smooth, shiny leaf. Its tiny feet seemed to change their grip without even slowing down.

"Like switching shoes!" Sam said.

"Exactly like switching shoes," said Tokay. "Cockroaches do the very same trick."

Sam made a face. "I don't love cockroaches very much."

"Nobody has to love every bug," said Tokay. "But they're still pretty amazing climbers. Claws for bark, sticky feet for glass."

An ant slipped on a dewdrop, wobbled, then grabbed on with its claws and kept right on marching, crumb and all.

"It's okay, little ant!" Sam cheered, cupping his hands like a megaphone. "You got it! Keep going!"

The ant line disappeared over the top of the wall, crumb safely delivered to wherever ants keep their crumbs.

"Where next?" Sam asked, bouncing on his toes.

Tokay pointed toward the big oak tree at the end of the yard, and past it, a tall gray shape Sam had never once seen in his own garden.

"That," said Tokay, "is a mountain. Just for tonight."

Sam's eyes went wide as dinner plates. "A whole entire mountain?!"

"Hold on tight," said Tokay, and they were off.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Goats on a Cliff
chapters.text:
The mountain was steep and gray, with hardly anywhere to stand. The wind up there smelled cold and sharp. Sam gulped. "Is it safe?"

"Watch," said Tokay.

A mountain goat trotted along a skinny ledge like it was just a sidewalk. Another goat stood balanced on a rock so small Sam could barely even see it.

"They're not scared at all!" Sam said.

"Goats have special hooves," said Tokay. "Hard on the edge, soft and squishy in the middle. The soft part squishes onto the rock and grips like a handshake."

Sam looked down at his own sneakers. "My shoes don't squish like that."

"Nope," laughed Tokay. "That's why you don't live on a cliff."

A baby goat hopped from rock to rock, following its mother without ever slowing down, sure-footed and happy.

"Go, baby goat, go!" Sam shouted, cupping his hands.

The goats reached a grassy ledge and started munching away, happy as could be, like cliffs were no big deal at all.

Sam let out a big breath he didn't know he was holding. "They made it look so easy."

"For goats," said Tokay, "it is easy."

Sam giggled. "Lucky goats. I want hooves like that."

Below them, the mountain melted back into Sam's own backyard fence, and the big oak tree stood where the cliff had just been.

"Oak tree!" said Sam. "I know that tree. Someone lives inside it."

He pointed at a gray, bushy tail flicking near the trunk.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Squirrel's Secret
chapters.text:
A squirrel zipped straight up the oak tree trunk, fast as a blink, her tail puffed out like a feather duster.

"How does she go so fast?" Sam asked.

"Claws," said Tokay. "Sharp, curved claws. They dig into tiny bumps and cracks too small for us to see."

Sam touched the tree bark. It felt smooth to him. "I don't see any cracks at all."

"That's the trick," said Tokay. "Her claws find cracks your fingers can't even feel."

The squirrel paused halfway up, looked down at them, and flicked her tail twice.

"Hi!" Sam waved. "You're really, really good at climbing."

The squirrel chattered back, like she was saying thank you, then zipped the rest of the way up and leaped onto a branch.

"She didn't even stop to catch her breath," Sam said, amazed.

"Squirrels practice every single day," said Tokay. "Up and down, up and down, their whole entire lives."

Sam nodded slowly. "Like how I practice my letters every day."

"Just like that," said Tokay, smiling.

A little acorn dropped and bonked Sam gently on the head.

"Ow! Hey!" Sam laughed, rubbing his head.

From up above, the squirrel chattered again, like she was laughing too.

"Let's find our next climber before she drops anything else," said Tokay, and they hurried toward the garden pond, where something small and green sat quietly on a lily pad.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Frog on the Leaf
chapters.text:
By the pond, a tiny green frog sat on a wet leaf, perfectly still, like he was thinking very hard about something.

"A frog!" said Sam. "Can frogs climb too?"

"Watch this one," said Tokay.

The frog hopped onto the glass side of the pond and stuck there, almost upside down, not sliding one single bit.

"Whoa, it's stuck like you!" Sam said.

"Not quite like me," said Tokay. "Tree frogs have flat toe pads covered in sticky slime, called **mucus**. The pads even have a tiny pattern underneath, little six-sided shapes, like a honeycomb."

Sam leaned in close. "Like bee honeycomb?"

"Just like that," said Tokay. "That pattern and the slime help the frog's toes hug wet leaves and glass without sliding away."

Sam grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. "Sticky slime feet. Hairy spider feet. Hairy gecko feet. Everybody's got a different trick!"

"Now you're getting it," said Tokay, looking proud as can be.

The little frog gave a small croak, like he agreed completely, then hopped off into the water with a tiny SPLOOSH.

Sam laughed so hard he nearly fell right over. "SPLOOSH! Do it again, froggy, do it again!"

But the frog was already swimming off, leaving tiny ripples spreading out behind him.

"One more stop," said Tokay, "before bedtime." He pointed to a shiny silver trail curling slowly across a garden stone.

"A trail?" Sam said. "Who made that squiggly thing?"

"Follow it," said Tokay, "and find out."

Sam followed, tiptoeing along the edge of the pond.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Slow and Slippery Snail
chapters.text:
The silver trail led to a snail, inching up the garden wall, slow and steady, like he had all night to get there.

"A snail? On a wall?" Sam said. "That seems impossible."

"Watch its belly," said Tokay.

The snail glided along on a layer of slime, its soft underside rippling in tiny waves, like a wiggly little dance.

"It's dancing up the wall!" Sam laughed.

"The slime lets its foot grip and slide at the very same time," said Tokay. "Slow, but it never, ever falls."

Sam watched the snail reach the top of the wall and tuck into its shell for a rest.

"Good job, snail," Sam whispered.

Tokay hopped up onto Sam's shoulder. "That's everyone for tonight. Geckos, spiders, flies, ants, goats, squirrels, frogs, and snails. Every single one climbs its own special way."

Sam counted on his fingers, one by one. "That's eight climbers!"

"Eight climbers," Tokay agreed. "And guess what? Some people liked our sticky gecko tricks so much, they made sticky gloves, copying gecko feet, so people could climb glass walls too."

Sam's eyes went huge. "People climbing like geckos?! That is the coolest thing I have ever heard."

"Maybe someday you'll climb like that," said Tokay. "But for now, it's bedtime."

A green door shimmered open in the garden wall, and through it Sam could see his own bedroom, soft and warm and waiting just for him.

Sam stepped through, bug jar still in hand, one sleepy roly-poly still snoozing inside it.

Tokay hopped back onto the shelf and froze into a toy once more, his eyes dimming down to two tiny dots.

But just before they went dark completely, Sam was almost sure he saw them wink.

Sam climbed into bed and pulled up his blanket, smiling up at the ceiling, like he half expected to see a few spiders up there too.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb high, and sleep tight.

fact_pack.summary: Lots of animals can climb smooth walls and even walk upside down on ceilings, using clever tricks like sticky pads, tiny hooked claws, or millions of microscopic hairs. Scientists who study these tricks have even copied them to invent new kinds of sticky tape and climbing gloves for people.

facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk across ceilings because their toes have millions of microscopic hairs called setae.
Each gecko seta splits into hundreds of even tinier tips called spatulae, which get so close to a surface that weak molecular attractions called van der Waals forces hold the foot in place.
A gecko's sticky grip is not glue, so its feet never get messy or leave residue, and it can lift its toes off instantly by peeling them, toe by toe, like pulling up tape.
Flies and some beetles climb using tiny pads on their feet that ooze a sticky liquid, acting like natural glue drops.
Spiders have thousands of microscopic hairs called setules on their feet, similar in idea to gecko hairs, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches use a combination of sharp claws for rough surfaces and sticky footpads for smooth ones, switching tools depending on the wall.
Mountain goats and some wild sheep climb near-vertical cliffs using hooves with a hard outer rim and a soft, grippy inner pad that molds to rock.
Squirrels climb trees and walls using sharp curved claws that dig into tiny cracks and bumps invisible to human eyes.
Tree frogs have special flattened, mucus-covered toe pads with tiny hexagon-shaped patterns that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Snails and slugs climb smooth walls by gliding on a layer of slime, which lets their muscular foot grip and move in rippling waves.
Some crabs and lobsters use small hooked bristles on their legs to cling to rocky, underwater walls against strong currents.
Bats cannot climb walls quickly like geckos, but they use curved claws on their feet to hang upside down from cave ceilings and cliff walls.
Woodpeckers climb straight up tree trunks using stiff tail feathers as a prop and two toes forward, two toes back for extra grip.
In 2014, scientists built a gecko-inspired handheld paddle that let a person climb a glass wall by pressing sticky synthetic pads against it.
Engineers have copied gecko foot structure to create reusable sticky tape and gripping robot feet that work in space, where regular glue fails in a vacuum.
A gecko's sticking ability is so strong that scientists calculated a gecko the size of a human could theoretically support its whole body weight from one finger, though real geckos are small.
Geckos keep their sticky feet clean and dust-free through a self-cleaning effect, where dirt particles roll off the tiny hairs as the gecko walks.
Praying mantises and stick insects use both small claws and sticky pads called arolia, choosing which one to use depending on the surface.
Some climbing animals, like certain ants, are so light compared to their sticky footpad area that they could theoretically hold many times their own body weight while hanging upside down.
Rock climbers sometimes study gecko and insect feet for ideas on new types of climbing shoes and gloves with better grip.
Many wall-climbing animals rely on physics tricks rather than suction, since true suction cups need airless pockets that are hard to maintain on rough or dusty surfaces.
Remoras, a type of fish, use a modified dorsal fin shaped like a suction pad to stick to sharks, whales, and boat hulls rather than walls.

story.title: Milo and Juno and the Brick That Started It All
story.subtitle: A tiny captain, a glowing brick, and the true story of LEGO.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Carpenter in Billund (1932)
chapters.text:
Milo stacked a LEGO shark on a LEGO wave. Juno stomped two dinosaur bricks across the rug, roaring.

It was way past bedtime. The floor was a whole city of bricks.

Then one brick, right by Milo's knee, began to glow green. It hummed. HMMMMM.

"Milo," whispered Juno. "That brick is awake."

Milo poked it. CLICK! The brick popped open like a tiny door. Out popped a tiny yellow man in a captain's hat.

"Ahoy!" he said. "I'm Captain Brick. Want to see where LEGO bricks came from? Hop on!"

Juno grabbed Milo's hand. The glow swallowed the whole room. WHOOOOSH!

They landed in a wooden workshop that smelled like sawdust. A man was carving a little wooden duck.

"That's Ole Kirk," said Captain Brick. "He started this whole toy company, in a town called **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**."

Milo picked up a wooden duck. "He only made wood toys?"

"At first," said Captain Brick. "Ole Kirk kept trying new things until they worked. That's how he was."

Juno hugged the duck. "I like him already."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well! (1934)
chapters.text:
Two years later, the workshop had a brand new sign going up outside.

BANG, BANG went the hammer.

"What does it say?" asked Juno, who could not read yet.

Ole Kirk smiled at them. "It says **LEGO**. I made that word up, in **1934**."

Milo squinted at the letters. "Lee-go?"

"From two Danish words," said Ole Kirk. "***Leg godt***. It means **'play well.'**"

Juno tried it out loud. "Play well!"

"Some people also say *lego* is an old Latin word that means 'I put together,'" said Captain Brick. "That might just be a fun coincidence. Nobody is totally sure. But it's a good story, so people love to tell it."

Milo grinned. "It fits anyway. You put LEGO bricks together."

"Exactly," said Captain Brick. "Play well. Put together. Both true."

The sign went up with a final CLANG. Everyone clapped, even the tiny captain.

"PLAY WELL!" shouted Juno, as loud as her dinosaur roar.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Plastic Surprise (1947)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! The workshop melted away. A big noisy machine took its place, going CHUGGA CHUGGA CHUGGA.

"What's that thing eating?" asked Milo, backing up a step.

"Plastic," said Captain Brick. "In **1947**, Ole Kirk got one of the very first machines in Denmark that could squirt hot plastic into shapes."

Juno watched a worker pour little plastic pellets in the top. They came out the other side as toy cars.

"Two years later," said Captain Brick, "in **1949**, they made a brand new toy. Hollow plastic bricks with bumps on top."

Milo picked one up. It had little round bumps, but underneath it was empty, like a cup turned upside down.

"They called them **Automatic Binding Bricks**," said Captain Brick. "Funny name. But look familiar?"

Milo pressed two together. They sort of stayed. Then he wiggled them, and they fell apart.

"Not quite there yet," he said.

"Not quite," agreed Captain Brick. "Somebody still has to fix that wobble."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Little Tubes, Big Click (1958)
chapters.text:
A man with a pencil was frowning at a brick on his desk.

"That's Godtfred," whispered Captain Brick. "Ole Kirk's son."

Milo flipped a brick over and looked at the empty space underneath. "What if something was in here," he said, "to hug the bumps on the brick below?"

Godtfred stared at him. Then he grabbed his pencil and drew little round tubes inside the bottom of the brick.

Juno lined up two new bricks and pressed down hard.

CLICK!

She pulled. It held tight.

"IT CLICKS!" the kids yelled together.

"That click you just heard," said Captain Brick, "got written down for real on **January 28, 1958**. That's the day the new brick design became official."

Milo tried stacking ten bricks in a wobbly tower. It didn't fall.

"Best part," said Captain Brick, "a brick from that very day still clicks perfectly with your bricks at home. The design barely changed at all."

Juno gasped. "So OLD bricks and MY bricks are friends?"

"Best friends," said Captain Brick.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Fresh Start (1960)
chapters.text:
The factory looked different now. No more wooden ducks on the shelves.

"Where did the wood toys go?" asked Milo.

"Something happened at the warehouse around **1960**," said Captain Brick gently. "The wooden toys stopped being made. Everyone was safe. And the company got to start fresh, with plastic bricks instead."

Juno looked around at shelf after shelf of colorful bricks. "Fresh start looks pretty great."

"It does," agreed Captain Brick. "Sometimes an ending helps something new begin."

Milo noticed the shelves were stuffed with red, blue, and yellow bricks, way more than before.

"Plastic bricks all the way now," he said.

"All the way," said Captain Brick, and gave the nearest shelf a happy little pat.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Brick Park (1968)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! Suddenly there were roller coasters made of tiny bricks, towering overhead.

"WHOA," said Milo. "Is this a whole PARK?"

"It is," said Captain Brick. "The very first **LEGOLAND** opened right here in Billund, in **1968**. Right next to the old factory."

Juno spotted a brick dinosaur as tall as a house. She ran right up to it.

"Look, don't touch," said Captain Brick kindly. "Even a brick dinosaur likes its space."

Juno waved at it instead. "Hello, big guy."

Milo counted little brick people riding a brick train. "Somebody built ALL of this out of bricks?"

"Every bit," said Captain Brick. "People still visit today."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Big Bricks for Little Hands (1969)
chapters.text:
A box on the floor said DUPLO in big letters. Juno tore it open.

The bricks inside were huge, easy for little fingers to grab.

"These came out in **1969**," said Captain Brick, "made just the right size for little kids like you, Juno."

Juno snapped a giant brick onto a giant brick. CLICK!

"And here's the fun part," said Captain Brick. "A DUPLO brick still clicks onto your regular LEGO bricks too."

Milo tried it. A tiny shark brick clicked right onto Juno's giant dinosaur tower.

"Shark meets dino!" Juno cheered.

"Big and small, always friends," said Captain Brick.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Tiny People, Big Hug (1978)
chapters.text:
Captain Brick held up something new. A tiny plastic person, with arms that moved and a hat that popped off.

"First one of these ever made," he said proudly. "**1978**. The very first LEGO minifigure."

Milo gasped. "That's basically YOU."

"Basically me," grinned Captain Brick, tipping his captain's hat.

Juno swapped the figure's hat for a tiny dinosaur head. Everyone laughed.

"Time to go home, you two," said Captain Brick softly. "This whole company still sits in Billund, right where Ole Kirk's workshop first stood."

WHOOOOSH! The green glow wrapped around them again.

They landed back on their own bedroom rug, bricks still scattered everywhere. The glowing brick sat quiet now, just a brick again.

But right beside it sat one tiny yellow minifigure, wearing a captain's hat.

Milo picked it up gently and set it on the shelf, ready for next time.

Juno yawned a dinosaur-sized yawn.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: **Ole Kirk Christiansen** started the company making wooden toys, in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**.
In **1934** he named the company **LEGO**, from Danish words meaning **'play well.'**
Some people also say *lego* is an old Latin word meaning 'I put together' — that might just be a fun coincidence.
In **1947** the company got a machine that could squirt hot plastic into toy shapes.
In **1949** they made hollow plastic bricks with bumps on top, called **Automatic Binding Bricks**.
**Godtfred**, Ole Kirk's son, added little tubes underneath the brick so it would click and hold tight, made official on **January 28, 1958**.
A brick from **1958** still clicks perfectly with bricks made today, because the design barely changed.
The first **LEGOLAND** park opened in Billund in **1968**, right by the old factory.
Big **DUPLO** bricks, sized for little hands, came out in **1969** and still click onto regular bricks.
The very first little LEGO **minifigure**, with bendy arms and a pop-off hat, appeared in **1978**.
The company still sits in **Billund, Denmark**, right where Ole Kirk's workshop first stood.

fact_pack.summary: LEGO began as a small Danish carpenter's workshop in 1932 and grew into one of the world's best-loved toys, built around a simple plastic brick that clicks together and never goes out of style. Along the way the company survived a warehouse fire and a near-bankruptcy, while keeping every brick compatible with every other brick ever made.

facts.text: Carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen founded the company in Billund, Denmark, in 1932, first making wooden toys and stepladders.
In 1934 Christiansen named his company LEGO, a shortening of the Danish phrase 'leg godt,' meaning 'play well.'
A popular story notes that 'lego' also happens to mean 'I put together' in Latin, though this seems to be a happy coincidence rather than the real reason for the name.
LEGO began working with plastic in 1947, becoming one of the first Danish companies to own a plastic injection-molding machine.
In 1949 the company produced 'Automatic Binding Bricks,' hollow studded plastic bricks that were the direct ancestor of the modern LEGO brick.
Ole Kirk's son Godtfred Kirk Christiansen redesigned the brick with hollow tubes underneath, and the new locking brick was patented on 28 January 1958.
A brick made in 1958 still fits perfectly with a LEGO brick made today because the tube-and-stud design has barely changed.
A 1960 fire destroyed the company's wooden-toy warehouse, and afterward the family decided to stop making wooden toys and focus only on plastic bricks.
In 1963 LEGO switched its brick material to ABS plastic, which resists cracking and keeps its color much better than the earlier plastic.
The first LEGOLAND theme park opened in Billund in 1968, right next to the original factory.
DUPLO bricks, sized just right for toddlers and still compatible with regular LEGO bricks, were introduced in 1969.
The LEGO Technic line, adding gears, axles and beams for more mechanical builds, launched in 1977.
The first LEGO minifigures, with movable arms and swappable heads and hats, appeared in 1978.
Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen, grandson of the founder, took over leadership of the company in 1979, keeping it in family hands for another generation.
Because so many tiny rubber tires are made for LEGO sets, the company is sometimes called one of the world's biggest tire producers by count, though it makes no full-size tires.
LEGO launched its first Star Wars sets in 1999, beginning a long line of licensed themes based on movies and games.
The Fortune Encyclopedia and other outlets named the LEGO brick a top 'Toy of the Century' around the year 2000.
In the early 2000s the LEGO Group ran into serious financial trouble and came close to bankruptcy.
Jorgen Vig Knudstorp became CEO in 2004 and led a turnaround that focused the company back on its core brick sets.
In 2014 The LEGO Movie brought LEGO characters to cinemas worldwide and became a major box-office success.
The LEGO Group is still headquartered in Billund, Denmark, on the same ground where Ole Kirk's workshop once stood.
The Kirkbi family, descendants of Ole Kirk Christiansen, remain the majority owners of the LEGO Group today.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow in the Hose
story.subtitle: A backyard spray turns into a light-bending adventure.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Backyard Sprinkle
chapters.text:
Dev squeezed his water pistol one more time before bed. **SPLOOSH!** A puff of spray floated up, gold from the low sun.

"Dev, you're making it rain sideways," said Priya, not looking up from her drawing of clouds.

Then the mist did something strange. It lit up every color at once, hanging there like a tiny glowing arch.

A drop the size of a marble popped out of the mist, swirling with color. "Hiya! I'm Pip," it said. "You made a rainbow — but you're facing the wrong way!"

"There's a wrong way?" said Dev.

"Sun has to be behind you, rain has to be in front," said Pip. "Spin around!"

Dev spun and sprayed again. A full little rainbow bowed over the fence.

"IT WORKED!" Dev shouted, and even Priya put down her pencil to look.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
Pip shrank them down smaller than a ladybug and tucked them inside one floating drop.

"Whoa," said Priya, pressing her hand against the curved wall. "It's like being inside a marble."

A beam of sunlight shot in through the top of the drop. It bent sideways the second it touched the water, like a straw looking crooked in a glass.

"Light slows down going into water," said Pip, "so it tips over, just a bit."

The light zoomed to the back of the drop and bounced off like a ball off a wall. Then it bent again on its way out, heading straight for Priya's eyes.

"It bends twice!" said Priya. "In, bounce, out!"

"Exactly," said Pip. "That bending is why we even get a rainbow at all."

Dev poked the drop's wall. "Can I bounce too?" Pip laughed so hard she rippled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Colors
chapters.text:
Outside the drop, Pip set a little triangle of glass on the fence. The sun hit it and sprayed color across the grass.

"That's a prism," said Pip. "Just a glass triangle that splits light apart."

"Splits it from what?" asked Dev.

"Sunlight looks white," said Pip, "but it's secretly every color squashed together."

Priya grinned. "Like when I mix all my paint colors and it goes muddy brown — except backward!"

"A scientist named **Isaac Newton** proved it, back in the **1660s**," said Pip. "He used a glass prism just like this one, and showed the colors were hiding inside the light the whole time."

Dev squirted his water pistol through the beam, and the colors jumped right onto the spray.

"I made a Newton!" Dev announced proudly.

"Close enough," said Priya, ruffling his hair.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Red Out, Purple In
chapters.text:
Pip lined up seven glowing ribbons of color in the air. "Quick, Priya — artist's job. Put these in order."

Priya tapped her chin, then pointed. "Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and then the purply ones."

"Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet," said Pip. "People remember it as **Roy G. Biv**."

"Like a name," said Dev. "Roy G. Biv. Hi, Roy."

"Here's the trick," said Pip. "Red always bends the least, so it ends up on the outside. Violet bends the most, so it tucks in on the inside."

Dev squinted at the backyard rainbow. "Red's on the outside! You were right, Pip!"

"I usually am," said Pip, spinning smugly, until Priya flicked a little water at it and it wobbled sideways, giggling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Whole Circle
chapters.text:
Pip lifted them up on a cushion of mist, higher than the roof.

"Whoa, where'd the bottom go?" said Dev, staring down.

From up here, the rainbow wasn't an arch anymore. It was a full, round ring of color, like a colorful donut floating over the yard.

"Rainbows are actually always circles," said Pip. "Down on the ground, the dirt and grass are in the way, so you only see the top half."

Priya leaned over the mist, careful not to lean too far. "So every rainbow I've ever seen was secretly a whole circle?"

"Every single one," said Pip.

Dev spread his arms like he was flying. "I'm inside a donut rainbow!"

They drifted gently back down before anyone got dizzy, both kids laughing the whole way.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Two Kids, Two Rainbows
chapters.text:
Back on the lawn, Pip had Priya stand by the rose bush and Dev stand by the gate.

"Dev, squirt the hose again," said Pip. "Priya, tell me what you see."

"I see a rainbow kind of... there," said Priya, pointing.

"I see one over *here*," said Dev, pointing somewhere totally different.

"You're both right," said Pip. "Every person sees their very own rainbow, made from different drops, because it depends exactly where you're standing."

"So mine's better," said Dev.

"They're exactly the same amount of good," said Priya, nudging him.

Then, above the first rainbow, a second, fainter one appeared, its colors flipped upside down.

"A twin!" gasped Priya. "But backward!"

"Light bounced twice inside those drops instead of once," said Pip. "That flips the colors around."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rainbows Everywhere
chapters.text:
"Does it only happen with hoses and rain?" asked Priya, already imagining a drawing.

"Nope," said Pip. "Waterfalls make them. Garden spray makes them. Even fog can, if the sun's right."

Dev gasped. "Water pistols count as spray!"

"Water pistols absolutely count," said Pip.

The sun had almost set now, and the first stars were out. "Can the moon make one too?" asked Priya.

"Sometimes," said Pip. "It's called a moonbow. Moonlight is so much dimmer than sunlight that moonbows usually look silvery-white instead of colorful to us."

"A secret rainbow," whispered Priya, delighted.

Dev gave one last squirt toward the moon, just in case. Nothing happened except a slightly damp Priya.

"Dev!" she yelped, laughing anyway.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The End of the Rainbow
chapters.text:
"So where does a rainbow actually end?" asked Dev. "Old stories say there's gold there."

"That's a fun old tale," said Pip, "but a rainbow doesn't have a real end spot. It moves exactly when you move, so you can never walk up and touch it."

"No treasure?" said Dev, a little disappointed.

Priya grinned. "You've got a water pistol and a rainbow guide. That's basically treasure."

Pip glowed warmly. "Spray bright, dream bright, you two."

The mist carried them gently back down to the same patch of grass where they'd started. Pip shrank to a single sparkling drop and slipped quietly into the garden hose.

Inside, Priya taped her new drawing to the wall: a round rainbow donut, with Dev's water pistol right in the middle of it.

"Night, Priya," mumbled Dev, already half asleep.

"Night, Roy G. Biv," she whispered back, grinning in the dark.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Spray bright, dream bright.

fact_pack.summary: Rainbows appear when sunlight passes through raindrops and gets bent, split into colors, and bounced back to our eyes. They are a science-and-wonder topic: a physics lesson dressed up as a beautiful arc in the sky, with plenty of fun details for kids to explore.

facts.text: A rainbow forms when sunlight enters a raindrop, bends, reflects off the inside back of the drop, and bends again as it exits.
This bending of light is called refraction, and it happens because light slows down and changes direction when it moves from air into water.
White sunlight is actually made of many colors mixed together, and raindrops separate them because each color bends by a slightly different amount.
The classic rainbow color order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet, often remembered with the name 'Roy G. Biv'.
Red always appears on the outer edge of a rainbow and violet on the inner edge because red bends the least and violet bends the most.
To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and rain (or spray) must be in front of you.
Rainbows are actually full circles, but we usually only see an arc because the ground blocks the bottom half.
From an airplane, people sometimes see a complete circular rainbow because there is no ground in the way.
Every person actually sees a slightly different rainbow, made from different raindrops, because the angle of light to your eyes is unique to your position.
A rainbow always appears in the part of the sky directly opposite the sun, centered on a point called the antisolar point.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow appears above the main one, with its colors reversed, caused by light bouncing twice inside the raindrops.
The dark strip of sky between a primary and secondary rainbow is called Alexander's band, named after the ancient Greek philosopher Alexander of Aphrodisias who described it around 200 AD.
Rainbows can also form in mist, waterfalls, garden hose spray, and even moonlight, where they are called moonbows.
Moonbows are usually so faint that they look white or gray to human eyes, though cameras can capture their colors.
The scientist Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s that a glass prism could split white light into the same rainbow of colors, proving light itself contains all the colors.
The Persian scientist Ibn al-Haytham and later Kamal al-Din al-Farisi studied light and rainbows in raindrops centuries before Newton, around the 1000s and 1300s.
Many cultures have myths about rainbows, such as the Norse story of Bifrost, a rainbow bridge connecting Earth to the home of the gods.
In the Bible, the rainbow appears as a sign of a promise from God to Noah after a great flood.
Many cultures tell of a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow, especially in Irish folklore involving leprechauns, though a rainbow's end is never a real fixed spot since it moves as you move.
Because a rainbow depends on where the viewer stands, you can never actually walk up to or touch one.
Rainbows need both sunlight and water droplets at the same time, which is why they often appear during or right after a rain shower when the sun peeks out.
A rainbow's size in the sky is always about the same, spanning roughly 42 degrees from the antisolar point for the primary bow.
The rainbow flag, created by artist Gilbert Baker in 1978, uses rainbow colors as a symbol of pride and diversity.
Rainbows are studied in a branch of science called optics, which explores how light behaves, bends, and reflects.

story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Glow-Tooth Dive
story.subtitle: A bedtime swim through four hundred million years of sharks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glow-Tooth Under the Bed
chapters.text:
Jack lined up his shark teeth on the carpet, biggest to smallest, for the hundredth time that week. Ellie sat beside him, brushing her mermaid doll's hair and humming a tune only she knew.

"Lights out in five minutes," Mom called from the hallway.

Jack grabbed his favorite tooth, a big gray triangle he'd found at the beach. That's when it happened. The tooth began to glow, soft blue-green, like a nightlight somebody forgot to switch off.

"Jack," Ellie whispered, "your tooth is doing a THING."

The glow spread across the carpet like spilled water. The carpet wasn't carpet anymore. It was cool, blue, and moving. A swirl of light opened at their feet.

WHOOOOSH!

Down they went, tooth and all, spinning through warm salty water.

When the spinning stopped, they floated in endless blue, next to a long gray fish with a flat body.

"Where ARE we?" Ellie asked, gripping Jack's sleeve.

"I think," Jack said slowly, "we're swimming with the very first sharks ever."

The old fish tilted its head. "Smart guess. My kind showed up more than **four hundred million years ago** — before the dinosaurs, before even the trees."

Jack reached out and gave its side a gentle poke. It didn't feel bony like a fish bone at the fish market. It felt bendy, like the top of his own ear.

"Your bones are squishy!" he said.

"Not squishy — bendy," the shark said. "It's called **cartilage**. The same stuff is in your ears and the end of your nose. No hard bones at all."

Ellie touched her own ear and grinned. "Mine bends too!"

"Exactly," said the shark. "Now — want to see how big sharks can get?"

Jack looked at Ellie. Ellie looked at Jack. Both nodded at the exact same time, which almost never happened.

"Follow the current," the shark said, and swam off into the blue.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Biggest Fish in the Sea
chapters.text:
A huge shadow rolled over them, blocking the sun like a cloud.

"Is that... a whale?" Ellie squeaked.

Jack grinned. "No way. Look at the spots. That's a whale SHARK."

The giant shark drifted by, its mouth open wide like a cave.

"How big IS it?" Jack called.

"Over **forty feet long**," said the old shark, catching up. "Biggest fish in the whole sea. But don't worry — it only eats tiny floating bits called **plankton**. It sucks in water like a straw and strains out its dinner."

Bubbles streamed from slits along its side.

"What are those?" Ellie asked.

"Gills," said the shark. "Slits it breathes through, same as all of us."

"It's gentle," Ellie said, surprised.

"Gentlest giant around," the shark agreed. "We never touch the big ones. Just watch."

Jack kept his hands tucked by his sides, careful, and Ellie did the same.

More shapes drifted past, including a shark with a head shaped like a hammer.

"That looks like a tool from Dad's garage!" Jack laughed.

"Hammerhead," said the guide. "Its eyes sit out on each side of that wide head. It sees almost all the way around itself."

"Like eyes in the back of its head!" Ellie said.

"Close enough," the shark chuckled. "There's over **five hundred kinds** of sharks out there — big, small, round, flat, spotted, striped."

Jack counted shapes on his fingers until he ran out of fingers. "I give up counting!"

Ellie giggled so hard a bubble popped out of her nose, and even the old shark seemed to laugh.

"Keep swimming," it said. "There's older stuff ahead."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Cave of Giant Teeth
chapters.text:
The water turned dim and cool, and rocky walls rose up on both sides.

"Where'd the sun go?" Ellie asked, pressing close to Jack.

"Just a deep spot," the old shark said. "Nothing to worry about. Look up there."

Stuck in the rock, glinting like treasure, were teeth. Not normal-sized teeth. Each one was as long as a hand.

Jack's mouth fell open. "Those are HUGE."

Ellie held her palm against one. It matched exactly.

"Those belonged to **Megalodon**," said the shark. "A giant shark from long, long ago. Way bigger than anything swimming today. It's not around anymore — that's called **extinct**, which just means none are left."

"Why are there only teeth?" Jack asked. "Where are its bones?"

"Remember the bendy stuff? Bendy bones don't turn to stone the way hard bone does. Only the teeth got left behind in the rock, kept safe for ages and ages. That's called a **fossil** — something very old, saved in the ground. Teeth are almost all we have to learn about Megalodon."

Ellie pulled her hand back from the tooth, careful not to touch too hard. "That might be a little scary, but it's mostly just amazing," she decided.

Jack nodded. "Good thing it's not swimming around anymore."

"Good thing," the shark agreed. "Now — want to know a secret about teeth that ARE still around today?"

Both kids shouted at once: "YES!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tooth Snowstorm
chapters.text:
A small gray shark swam past, and something fell from its mouth, drifting down like snow.

"Did its tooth just FALL OUT?" Jack gasped, catching it in his palm.

"Happens all the time," said the old shark. "Sharks lose teeth their whole life — **thousands** of them."

Ellie peered at the shark's mouth as it swam by again. "Won't it run out?"

"Never. New teeth keep moving forward, row after row, like a conveyor belt at the grocery store. Lose one in front, another slides up to take its place."

Jack turned the tooth over in his hand, smooth and white. "So this shark's got a whole closet of spare teeth?"

"More like an army," the shark said, "always ready."

Ellie wiggled her own loose front tooth, the one she'd been proud of all week. "I only get ONE new tooth each time!"

"Lucky you," Jack teased. "Imagine losing a thousand teeth and Mom trying to find the tooth fairy's address."

Ellie giggled so hard she forgot all about the dim, cool water from before.

"Keep the tooth," the old shark told Jack. "A gift, from one collector to another."

Jack tucked it carefully beside his glowing one. "Best souvenir ever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sandpaper Skin and Super Speed
chapters.text:
Something brushed Jack's arm, rough like sandpaper.

"Ow — well, not ow, just... weird," Jack said, rubbing his arm.

"That's shark skin," said the old shark. "Covered all over in tiny tooth-shaped bits. Rough like sandpaper, but it helps a shark slide through water fast, almost without any drag."

Ellie touched her mermaid doll's smooth tail and frowned. "Mermaids have smooth tails. Sharks have scratchy ones?"

"Different jobs," the shark said. "Smooth looks pretty. Scratchy helps you win a race."

As if to prove it, a silver shape shot past so fast the water shook.

"WHOA! What was THAT?" Jack shouted.

"Shortfin mako," the old shark said. "Fastest shark in the whole sea. Quick bursts of speed to catch fast fish like tuna."

Jack tried swimming after it and gave up after two kicks, laughing. "No way I'm catching that."

"Nobody is," the shark said. "Not even the tuna, most days."

Ellie patted Jack's shoulder. "Good thing you're not a tuna."

"Good thing," Jack agreed, still a little out of breath.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Weirdo Parade
chapters.text:
A small spotted shark waddled across the rocks below, using its fins like tiny paddles.

Ellie burst out laughing. "It's WALKING! Sharks don't walk!"

"This one does," said the old shark. "Epaulette shark. Walks right over reefs and puddles when the tide goes out. It can go for hours with barely any air to breathe."

Jack wiggled his arms like fins, walking in place in the water. Ellie copied him, and they both looked thoroughly ridiculous, which was entirely the point.

Further along, a wide flat shark lay still on the sandy bottom.

"Is it asleep?" Jack asked.

"Resting," the guide said. "Nurse shark. It pumps water over its gills while it lies still, so it doesn't have to keep swimming just to breathe."

"Lucky," Ellie said. "I have to keep moving my legs in the pool or I sink."

One more shark slid by, sleek and gray.

"That one," the old shark said, "is a bull shark. It swims in salty ocean water AND in rivers, far upstream, where the water isn't salty at all."

Jack blinked. "A shark... in a RIVER?"

"Far from the sea," the shark confirmed. "Tough customer."

Ellie shook her head slowly. "Sharks are weirder than mermaids, and that's saying something."

Jack grinned. "Called it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
A diver appeared ahead of them, moving easily through the water, trailing a notebook on a cord.

"Who's that?" Jack whispered.

"A good friend," the old shark said. "Eugenie Clark. Folks called her the **Shark Lady**. She spent her whole life studying sharks and proved they're curious — even trainable, like a very large, very toothy puppy."

The diver waved and swam over, smiling behind her mask.

Ellie spotted something leathery drifting near the sand, dark and shaped like a little pouch with curly strings at the corners.

"What's THAT?" she asked, pointing but not touching.

"Go on, pick it up gently," said Eugenie Clark.

Ellie cupped it in both hands. "It feels like a purse!"

"That's exactly what people call it — a **mermaid's purse**. Some sharks lay their eggs inside cases just like that one."

Ellie hugged it to her chest. "A real mermaid's purse. I KNEW mermaids and sharks were friends."

Jack had a question of his own. "Are sharks... dangerous? Like, to people?"

"Hardly ever," Eugenie Clark said. "Shark attacks on people are **very rare**. Way more sharks get hurt by people than the other way around."

"So they're not the bad guys," Jack said slowly.

"Far from it," she said. "Sharks sit at the top of the ocean's whole team, keeping everything else balanced and healthy. Lose the sharks, and the whole sea gets wobbly."

Jack nodded, satisfied. "Top of the team. Got it."

Eugenie Clark tucked her notebook away. "Time for you two to head home now. But keep being curious. That's half of it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Carpet
chapters.text:
The blue water began to spin again, faster and faster, pulling Jack and Ellie up and up.

"WAIT, I'M NOT DONE COUNTING SHARKS!" Jack yelled into the swirl.

"HOLD YOUR PURSE TIGHT!" Ellie yelled back, both arms wrapped around the leathery little pouch.

Then — THUMP. They landed softly, right back on the bedroom carpet, exactly where they'd started.

Jack's tooth necklace lay glowing faintly beside him, then went dark, just a plain gray tooth again.

Ellie opened her hands. Sitting right there on the carpet, real as anything, was the little leathery pouch.

"It came WITH us," she whispered.

Jack grinned, picking up his new spare tooth from the mako-fast shark and setting it beside his collection. "Best souvenirs ever. A tooth AND a mermaid's purse."

"Mermaids and sharks," Ellie said sleepily, "are definitely friends."

From the hallway, Mom's voice called again. "Lights out, you two!"

Jack flicked off his flashlight. Ellie tucked the little purse under her pillow, right next to her mermaid doll, already drifting toward sleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim safe, little fish.

story.title: Leo and the Dream Express
story.subtitle: A Nighttime Journey to Discover Why We Sleep

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Hoot Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Leo lay under his blanket. He liked his toy trains. He liked his toy owls too.

But the room felt very dark. He pulled the blanket up to his chin.

On his shelf sat Hoot, his little owl lamp. Hoot's eyes were shut, like always.

Tonight, Hoot's eyes popped open. They glowed soft gold. "Hello, Leo," Hoot said. "Want to see why everyone sleeps?"

Leo sat straight up. "Even owls?" he asked.

"Even owls," said Hoot. "Hop on."

A little train chugged out from under the bed. It was the Dream Express. Leo climbed aboard. The train went CHUFF, CHUFF, CHUFF, and the dark room melted into soft blue night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Twitchy Eyes (1953)
chapters.text:
The train stopped at an old science room.

Two men watched a sleeping boy. His eyes jiggled under his eyelids.

"Look!" said Leo. "His eyes are wiggling!"

"Good eyes, Leo," said Hoot. "In **1953**, two scientists named **Aserinsky** and **Kleitman** watched eyes do just that."

"They found a kind of sleep called **REM**," Hoot said. "REM means your eyes move fast while you dream."

Leo grinned. "So wiggly eyes mean dreaming!"

"Exactly," said Hoot. "You found it first."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Hills and Loops
chapters.text:
The train went up a hill, then down. Up and down, over and over.

"Why do we go up and down?" asked Leo.

"Sleep is like this track," said Hoot. "Every **ninety minutes**, your brain goes from quiet sleep to busy dream sleep. Up and down, all night long."

Leo watched the hills. "Like a roller coaster!"

"A sleepy roller coaster," Hoot laughed.

The train climbed one more hill, and Leo cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Limp Noodle
chapters.text:
At the top of a hill, the train got wobbly. Leo's arms flopped like noodles.

"Whoa!" said Leo. "I can't move!"

"That's REM sleep," said Hoot. "Your brain is busy, almost like when you're awake. But your body goes still, so you don't act out your dreams."

Leo giggled, floppy. "Like a wet noodle."

"A wet noodle brain party," said Hoot. "And deep, quiet sleep helps you grow, too. It's like a nighttime power-up."

Leo smiled sleepily. "I'm growing right now?"

"Every night," said Hoot.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sleepy Animal Windows
chapters.text:
The train rolled past windows full of animals.

A dolphin swam by with one eye open. "Dolphins sleep with only half their brain," said Hoot. "One half rests. One eye watches."

Next came a giraffe, standing tall. "Giraffes barely nap," said Hoot. "Sometimes under two hours a day!"

Then a tiny bat zoomed past, yawning. "Bats sleep **twenty hours**," said Hoot. "They are the sleepiest of all."

Leo laughed. "I want to be a bat today!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Night Clock
chapters.text:
The train chugged into a cozy clock tower.

"This clock keeps your body's time," said Hoot. "It's called your **circadian** clock. That means it follows about one whole day."

A tiny light blinked on the clock. "That's **melatonin**," said Hoot. "A sleepy helper made inside you. Scientists found it in **1958**."

Leo yawned. "I feel the sleepy helper working."

"Right on time," Hoot said, smiling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Boy Who Stayed Awake
chapters.text:
At a quiet station, Leo saw a teenager yawning hugely.

"That's Randy," said Hoot. "A long time ago, he tried staying awake for many days, to help scientists learn."

"Was he okay?" asked Leo, a little worried.

"He was fine," said Hoot. "But doctors say nobody should ever try that. Sleep keeps your brain happy and strong."

Leo nodded firmly. "I would miss my pillow too much."

Hoot chuckled. "Smart choice."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to Bed
chapters.text:
The Dream Express rolled home, past stars and soft clouds.

"Sleep also tucks away your memories," said Hoot. "Like packing today's fun into a cozy box for tomorrow."

The train slid under Leo's bed with a gentle SHHHH.

Leo blinked. He was back in his room. Hoot sat on the shelf, eyes glowing warm and low.

"Did I dream all that?" Leo asked.

"Maybe," said Hoot. "But now you know why we sleep."

Leo hugged his blanket, no longer scared of the dark.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. Fly soft, sleep tight.
