story.title: Ben and the Secret History of Games
story.subtitle: Ben presses start on the whole history of video games.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Wiggly Line Game (1958)
chapters.text:
Ben sat cross-legged on his bedroom floor, finishing a pixel-art dragon on his tablet. Square by square, green and black, it was almost done.

The clock said way past bedtime. Ben didn't care. He tapped in one more green pixel for the dragon's eye.

Then the screen went black. A second later it flashed green, like grass blocks at midnight. Ben blinked hard.

A small blocky shape popped right out of the screen. It was made of glowing squares, like someone had built a tiny person out of blocks.

"Hiya," said the shape. "Name's Byte. I live in screens. Also, I'm kind of obsessed with games. Wanna see where they came from?"

Ben's dragon was forgotten. "Wait. Games came from somewhere?"

"Oh, for sure," said Byte. "Every game's got an origin story. Press start?"

The air fizzed like static on an old TV. Ben's bedroom melted away into a big room full of humming machines.

"Whoa," said Ben. "Where are we now?"

"**Brookhaven National Laboratory**," said Byte. "Out in New York. The year is **1958**."

A man in glasses fiddled with a round glowing screen. A line wiggled across it, bright green, like a worm made of light.

"That's an **oscilloscope**," said Byte. "A machine that draws wiggly lines, kind of like a tiny TV for scientists."

The man, **William Higinbotham**, turned a dial. A little dot bounced along the line, back and forth, back and forth.

Ben leaned in close. "Is that... tennis?"

"Pretty much," said Byte. "He even calls it **'Tennis for Two.'**"

Higinbotham handed Ben a box with a dial and one button.

Ben turned the dial, lined up the bouncing dot, and pressed the button at just the right second. **BOOP!** The dot zipped back across the screen.

"You've got good hands," said Higinbotham, smiling.

Ben grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. "I just played the very first video game. Kind of."

"Kind of," agreed Byte. "This was way before controllers had buttons like yours. People lined up for hours just to get a turn."

Ben pressed the button one more time, just because he could. **BOOP!**

"Onward," said Byte, and the wiggly green line stretched wide and swallowed them both.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Spaceships in a Fridge-Sized Computer (1962)
chapters.text:
They landed with a soft THUMP in a room full of beeping machines, each one as big as a refrigerator.

"Where now?" asked Ben, stepping around a tangle of wires.

"**MIT**," said Byte. "A famous science school. The year is **1962**."

A student named **Steve Russell** sat tapping away at a computer so huge it filled a whole wall.

"That's a computer?" Ben said. "It's enormous!"

"Computers used to be giant," said Byte. "No phones in pockets yet. This one's called a **PDP-1**."

On a round screen, two tiny spaceships spun around and shot at each other.

"Whoa, is that a game?" Ben asked, pointing.

"**Spacewar!**," said Steve, grinning over his shoulder. "Me and my friends made it. Wanna fly one?"

Ben grabbed a set of switches. He spun his ship left, dodged a laser, and fired back.

"Watch the star in the middle," warned Steve. "Get too close and it pulls your ship right in."

Ben steered wide around the star, the same way he'd swing wide around lava in a cave. His ship zipped past Steve's and — **ZAP** — he scored a hit.

"Got you!" Ben cheered.

Steve laughed and leaned back in his chair. "Nobody outside this lab has even seen this game yet. You might be one of the first kids ever to play it."

"They will see it though," said Byte. "This is one of the very first computer games ever made, and people are going to love it."

Ben patted the giant, humming machine like a pet. "Good job, big guy. Keep doing your thing."

"Let's go," said Byte, "before Ben challenges him to round two and we're here all night."

"One more game?" Ben asked hopefully.

"Nope," said Byte, already glowing brighter. "History's calling, and it does not wait for rematches."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Brown Box in the Basement (1972)
chapters.text:
Next they popped into a cluttered workshop. Wires covered every table, and half-built boxes sat in stacks.

"Who lives here?" asked Ben, stepping over a loose cable.

"**Ralph Baer**," said Byte. "Folks later call him the **father of video games**. He had one big idea: play games right on your own TV, not just in a lab or an arcade."

Ralph held up a plain brown box with two wires hanging off it.

"That's... kind of boring looking," Ben admitted.

"Looks boring. Works magic," said Ralph, plugging it into a television. Two white squares and a little dot blinked onto the screen.

"Is that... Pong?" Ben asked.

"Close," said Ralph. "This is my test version — a **prototype**, which just means the very first try at something. I call it the **Brown Box**."

He handed Ben a controller. Ben nudged his square up, bounced the dot, and grinned when it bonked off the wall.

"Can everyone get one of these someday?" Ben asked.

"Soon," said Ralph. "In **1972**, this box becomes a real toy anyone can buy — the **Magnavox Odyssey**. The very first game console made just for home TVs."

Ben's jaw dropped. "Wait, that means somebody's living room turned into the very first home arcade!"

"Exactly," said Byte. "No quarters needed. Just your own couch and your own TV."

Ben bounced the little dot one more time. **BONK.** It hit the edge and swung back, and he caught it without even trying.

"I'm basically a pro at this already," Ben said, puffing his chest out.

Ralph chuckled, patting the brown box like an old friend. "That's the whole idea. Games anyone can play, right at home."

Byte tugged Ben's sleeve. "Speaking of anyone — somebody else had almost the exact same idea this very same year. Let's go meet him."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Machine That Ate Too Many Quarters (1972)
chapters.text:
They landed in a noisy, blinking room full of machines — an **arcade**, which is just a shop packed with game machines you pay to play.

"**Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari**," said Byte. "Same year as the Odyssey — **1972**. They built this one right here."

A wooden machine stood in the corner, screen glowing. Two paddles. One ball. **BEEP. BOOP.**

"It's kind of like Ralph's game, but for quarters," Ben said, peering at the coin slot.

"You got it," said Byte. "This one's called **Pong**."

Ben dropped in a quarter. **CLUNK.** He bounced the ball past the other paddle. **BEEP!**

"One more game!" Ben said, already feeding in another coin.

Just then a worker walked over, frowning at the machine. "It's jammed again," he muttered, prying open the coin box. Quarters spilled out onto the floor, clinking everywhere like rain.

Ben's eyes went wide. "It broke because of too many quarters?!"

"That's the story people tell," said Byte. "Nobody's totally sure it's true, but it shows just how fast folks fell head over heels for this game."

Ben scooped up a few rolling quarters and handed them back to the worker. "Guess everybody wanted a turn."

"Everybody," Byte agreed. "Arcades popped up on practically every corner after this."

Ben peeked through a gap at the machine's insides — wires, switches, little blinking lights. "It's kind of like redstone," he said, thinking of his own builds back home. "Simple parts, but they make something awesome happen."

"Exactly like that," said Byte, smiling. "Ready for round two of history?"

Ben slotted his very last quarter in. **BEEP BOOP BEEP.** "Ready."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: One Box, Any Game You Want (1977)
chapters.text:
The arcade faded into a cozy living room with a boxy TV in the corner.

"**1977**," said Byte. "Atari made something brand new — the **Atari 2600**."

Ben spotted a slot on the front of the console and a stack of plastic cases nearby.

"What are those?" he asked, picking one up and turning it over.

"**Cartridges**," said Byte. "Plastic cases you plug in to swap games. One box, loads of different games, instead of just one game stuck inside forever."

Ben slid a cartridge into the slot. **CLICK.** The TV blinked to life with a brand-new game.

"That's like changing a — " Ben stopped himself, eyes lighting up. "Wait, that's basically what loading a new world is, but with games instead of worlds!"

"Kind of exactly like that!" said Byte. "Go on, try swapping again."

Ben popped in another cartridge. The screen filled with little alien shapes, marching down in tidy rows like a parade.

"**Space Invaders**," said Byte. "Made in **1978** by **Tomohiro Nishikado**. It was such a huge hit that arcades everywhere wanted a machine of their own."

Ben grabbed the controller and blasted the aliens row by row, left to right, matching the way they marched.

"They're speeding up!" Ben said, firing faster and faster.

"They always do, the fewer of them there are," said Byte. "Keeps you right on your toes."

Ben zapped the very last alien. **PEW!** The screen flashed WIN in big letters.

"So one console, tons of cartridges, means tons of totally different games," Ben said slowly, nodding. "That's actually genius."

"Genius," agreed Byte. "Let's see what came next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Pizza, Ghosts, and a Buried Treasure (1980\u20131983)
chapters.text:
A yellow circle filled the screen, chomping dots as it zoomed through a maze.

"Meet **Pac-Man**," said Byte. "Made in **1980** by **Toru Iwatani**."

"Why's he just a mouth with a body?" Ben asked, laughing.

"Funny story," said Byte. "Some folks say Iwatani got the idea from a pizza missing one slice. Nobody's totally sure that's really true, but it's a fun thought to munch on."

Ben grabbed the joystick and guided Pac-Man around a corner, gobbling dots, dodging a ghost by a hair.

"Ha! Too slow, ghost!" Ben cheered, weaving through the maze.

But then the room flickered, and shelves of game cartridges appeared, piled high, with nobody around to buy them.

"What happened here?" Ben asked, looking at the dusty boxes.

"**1983**," said Byte. "Too many rushed, not-so-great games got made all at once. Stores ended up with way more games than people wanted to buy. Folks call it the **video game crash** — not an actual car crash, just a fancy way of saying the games business shrank fast."

Ben frowned at the dusty shelves. "That's kind of sad."

"A little," said Byte. "But don't worry, it gets better soon. Some of those unsold game cartridges even got buried in the ground out in New Mexico. People dug them back up again in **2014**, years and years later, like buried treasure."

Ben's eyes lit up. "Buried game cartridges? That's basically loot in a chest!"

"Pretty much exactly that," said Byte. "Speaking of treasure, somebody's about to dig this whole business back out of trouble."

Ben gave the dusty old Pac-Man machine a gentle pat. "Don't worry, buddy. Someone's coming to save game night."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Plumber and Some Falling Blocks (1984\u20131985)
chapters.text:
They landed inside a toy store, boxes stacked high on every shelf, a shiny gray console sitting front and center.

"**Nintendo**," said Byte, "brought games back strong. **1985**. Say hello to the **NES**."

Ben turned a box over in his hands. A mustached man in overalls jumped across the cover art.

"Who's this guy?" Ben asked.

"**Mario**," said Byte. "Designed by **Shigeru Miyamoto**. A plumber who jumps on things. He's about to become gaming's most famous face on the whole planet."

Ben popped the cartridge in and grabbed the controller. He ran Mario across the screen, jumped a gap, and bonked a question-mark block from underneath. **DING!** A coin popped out, spinning.

"Yes!" Ben shouted. "Again!"

He hopped over a mushroom-shaped enemy, landed neatly on a green pipe, and the screen scrolled onward to reveal more level.

"This feels like the first level of forever," Ben said, grinning ear to ear.

"Funny you say that," said Byte. "A year earlier, in **1984**, someone else invented a game that never really ends either."

The screen flickered to show colorful blocks falling and stacking neatly into rows.

"**Tetris**," said Byte. "Made by **Alexey Pajitnov** in Moscow. You stack the falling blocks. Whenever a whole row fills up, it disappears."

Ben rotated a block, slid it sideways, and slotted it in just right. A whole row vanished with a satisfying **ZIP**.

"That's so satisfying," Ben said happily. "It's like building, except the building kind of fights back a little."

"Couldn't have put it better myself," said Byte. "Two totally different games, one year apart, and people are still playing both of them today."

Ben cleared one more row before Byte pulled him onward. **ZIP!**

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Speedy Blue and a Shiny Disc (1991\u20131994)
chapters.text:
A blue blur zipped past so fast Ben nearly toppled over.

"Whoa, slow down!" Ben laughed, steadying himself.

The blur skidded to a stop in a puff of dust. Spiky blue, bright red shoes, arms crossed like he owned the place.

"**Sonic the Hedgehog**," said Byte. "Made by **Sega** in **1991**, built to be fast — faster than a certain plumber we just met."

Ben raced Sonic down a loop-the-loop track, collecting shiny golden rings as he went. **WHOOSH!**

"He's basically Minecraft on sprint, with an ender pearl in each pocket," Ben panted, trying to keep up.

Sonic winked and vanished in a streak of blue, leaving nothing but rings spinning in the air.

Next, the room filled with the soft whir of computers, and kids sat typing side by side, screens all glowing the same color.

"**1993**," said Byte. "A game called **Doom** let players battle each other on different computers, all hooked up together. Folks called it a **LAN party** — that just means a bunch of friends, all playing the same game together, in the same room."

"Like when my cousin brings his laptop over and we play side by side," Ben said.

"Exactly like that," said Byte, nodding.

The scene shifted again, to a shelf lined with shiny silver discs.

"**1994**," Byte went on. "**Sony** jumped into the console business with the **PlayStation**. It used discs instead of cartridges, which let games look and sound way better than before."

Ben held up a disc, watching it flash rainbow colors as it caught the light.

"It's like a mini DVD," Ben said, turning it over carefully.

"Pretty much," said Byte. "Fuller sound. Better graphics. Bigger adventures."

Ben slid the disc in and the screen roared to life with music and color.

"Onward," said Byte, "to the game you already know best of all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: A Block World and a Trophy Case (2006\u2013Today)
chapters.text:
A living room appeared, and a remote floated toward Ben, waggling on its own.

"**2006**," said Byte. "Nintendo made the **Wii**. Its remote watches how you move your arm, so swinging it really swings your character's bat too."

Ben swung the remote like a bat. Onscreen, a tiny character swung too, and a ball sailed off the screen.

"That's wild," Ben said. "It's like the controller's reading my mind!"

"Just your arm," laughed Byte. "Close enough."

The room melted into blocky green hills, blue sky, square clouds.

Ben gasped. "Wait — I KNOW this place!"

"**2011**," said Byte. "A developer named **Markus Persson**, folks call him **Notch**, released **Minecraft**. It went on to become the most ever sold video game in the whole world."

Ben spun in a circle, laughing. "This is literally my favorite place on Earth. Or, you know. Off Earth."

He punched a block of dirt. It popped loose exactly like always. He stacked three blocks and climbed up, same as every night at home.

"Still works the same everywhere," Ben said happily.

One more flicker, and they stood in a bright museum hall, glass cases glowing.

"The **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," said Byte. "Opened in **2015**, in Rochester, New York. All our old friends are in here."

Ben spotted Pac-Man's maze, a Mario cartridge, a Tetris screen, all lit up behind glass.

"They all end up here?" Ben asked.

"The best ones do," said Byte. "Maybe your pixel dragon someday."

Ben grinned at that. "Maybe."

The green flicker swirled around them, and the museum melted away. Ben blinked — and he was back on his bedroom floor, tablet glowing softly in his lap.

His pixel dragon was finished on the screen, every square in place, like it had waited for him.

"Night, Byte," Ben whispered.

Somewhere in the screen, one tiny block blinked back at him, green then dark.

Ben pulled his blanket up and closed his eyes, dreaming of plumbers, hedgehogs, and one blocky green world waiting for morning.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Press start on tomorrow.

story.title: Theo and the Glitch That Ate the Screen
story.subtitle: One midnight loading bar, eight levels of game history, and a pixel named Byte

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Green Dot at Brookhaven (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was supposed to be asleep two hours ago. Instead he was under a blanket tent, nudging a jump pad three pixels to the left in his half-finished Roblox obby.

He hit PLAY to test it. The screen didn't load his game. It went black, then flickered green, like an old TV melting into static.

"Hey—" Theo tapped the trackpad. Nothing happened.

Then a small blocky shape popped out of the glitch and hovered over his desk — bright green pixels stacked into a stubby-armed smiley face.

"Finally," it said. "Do you know how long I've been stuck at a low refresh rate?"

Theo nearly fell off his bed. "What *are* you?"

"Call me Byte," the sprite said, spinning once like a loading icon. "I live in the space between every video game ever made. Lucky you — your screen glitched straight into my neighborhood."

"Prove it," Theo said, because that's what you say to a floating pixel at midnight.

Byte snapped his stubby fingers. The glow swallowed the room.

When it cleared, Theo stood in a lab full of humming machines, facing a round glowing screen like a little porthole — an **oscilloscope**, a machine built to watch electricity draw pictures. On it, two flat lines and a glowing dot bounced back and forth.

"Want a turn?" A man in a short-sleeved shirt adjusted a dial. "Name's Bill."

Theo recognized it instantly. "That's tennis? That's the *whole* game?"

"That's it," Bill said, handing him a control box with a dial and a button. "Figured visitors needed something to do besides stare at physics charts."

Theo spun the dial. The dot arced over the middle line. He mashed the button at just the right second — the dot bounced back.

"Nice return," Bill said.

"When is this?" Theo asked.

"**1958**," Byte said, floating by his ear. "**William Higinbotham** built 'Tennis for Two' right here at **Brookhaven National Laboratory**. First video game anybody could actually sit down and play."

Theo kept the rally going four more hits before the dot drifted past him. "That's older than my grandpa's car."

"Everything starts somewhere," Byte said. "Ready to see where it went?"

Theo was already reaching for the glowing edge of the portal.

chapters.heading: Level 2: Spaceships on a Computer the Size of a Fridge (1962)
chapters.text:
The portal spat Theo out in a cramped room that smelled like warm electronics. A machine the size of a refrigerator buzzed in the corner, its round screen no bigger than a dinner plate.

Two guys in thick glasses argued over a sketch taped to the wall — two needle-shaped spaceships circling a dot.

"That's a star, right?" Theo asked, pointing. "It's pulling the ships in?"

A guy with a pencil behind his ear looked up, surprised. "Steve Russell," he said, shaking Theo's hand. "And yeah — kid's right. Gravity well. Fly too close, it eats your ship."

"So dodge it," Theo said, grabbing a spare control box full of toggle switches.

On screen, his needle-ship swung wide around the glowing dot, using its own pull to sling around faster — then fired a torpedo that caught the other ship clean.

"SWING AROUND THE STAR!" Theo yelled, pumping a fist.

Steve laughed. "That's exactly the move we hoped somebody would find."

"This is **1962**," Byte said. "**Steve Russell** and his friends at **MIT** just wrote 'Spacewar!' on this thing — a computer called a **PDP-1**, basically a fridge-sized brain that cost more than a house."

Theo looked at the sketch again, then at his own hands still gripping switches instead of a controller. "No joystick?"

"Give it time," Byte said. "Those come later. For now — switches, and whoever's fastest wins."

Theo flew two more rounds, lost once, won once, and grinned the whole time. "This is basically the first PvP game," he said. "People were gonna go nuts for this."

"They did," Byte said. "Next stop — somebody's about to figure out how to bring this home."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Box in Ralph's Basement (1972)
chapters.text:
The next room had wires running everywhere, all plugged into an ordinary television like the one in Theo's living room.

A man knelt behind it, soldering iron in hand, muttering to himself.

"You're building a game that plays on a regular TV?" Theo asked. "Not one of those lab screens?"

The man looked up. "Ralph Baer," he said. "And that's the whole idea. Why should games live in a laboratory? People have TVs at home."

He handed Theo a wooden box covered in switches — a rough first-try version, what Byte called a **prototype**. On the TV, two white squares and a dot appeared.

Theo flicked switches, and his square drifted sideways, wobbling. "It's kind of loose," he said. "Feels like it slides too far."

Ralph frowned, then adjusted a dial inside the box. "Better?"

Theo tried again. The square snapped to a stop exactly where he wanted it. "Way better."

"Good catch," Ralph said, scribbling a note.

"This is the late **1960s**," Byte said. "Ralph Baer — people later call him 'the father of video games' — is building the **'Brown Box'** right here. It becomes the **Magnavox Odyssey** in **1972** — the very first video game console anyone could own."

Theo turned the box over in his hands. "So this is where consoles started. Before this, nobody had one of these at home?"

"Nobody," Byte confirmed. "This box is the reason you have a shelf of them."

Theo set it down gently, like it might still be warm from the soldering iron. "Thanks for fixing the sliding thing for me," Ralph called after him.

"Anytime," Theo said, and meant it.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Machine That Ate Its Quarters (1972)
chapters.text:
The portal dumped Theo into a dim bar that buzzed with electricity and clinking coins. A wooden cabinet in the corner had a line of people waiting their turn.

"PONG," read the sign on top, next to two paddles and a bouncing square.

"Nolan Bushnell," said a man with a mustache, sticking out his hand. "This one's mine — well, mine and Ted Dabney's. We just started a company. Called it Atari."

Theo dropped a coin in and grabbed a paddle knob. The square zipped across the screen. He twisted it hard, sent the ball screaming back, and the machine let out a happy **BEEP-BOOP**.

"This is **1972**," Byte said. "**Atari**, founded by **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**, just released **Pong** in arcades, and it is about to be everywhere."

A kid behind Theo groaned. "Machine's stuck again. Too many quarters."

Nolan laughed, shaking his head. "Story goes one of our very first machines actually jammed solid — quarters just packed in, all the way up."

"Seriously?" Theo asked.

"That part might get told a little bigger every year," Byte admitted. "But jammed or not, people could not stop feeding that machine money. That part's completely true."

Theo watched the line behind the cabinet stretch out the door. "So this is basically when games became, like, a whole *thing*."

"Pretty much," Byte said. "One ball, two paddles, and the whole world wanted a turn."

Theo took one more match, won it on a lucky bounce off the top wall, and raised both fists before Byte tugged him toward the next glow.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Box You Could Swap (1977)
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like a toy store at Christmas. Shelves were stacked with flat plastic rectangles, and a console sat open on a counter with a slot in the front.

Theo picked one up. It looked exactly like a cartridge for an old-school console he'd seen in videos. "Wait — you can just pull the game out and put in a different one?"

"That's the whole point," said the shopkeeper, sliding one rectangle out and snapping another in. "One box, hundreds of games."

"This is **1977**," Byte said. "The **Atari 2600** just launched, and these plastic **cartridges** mean you're not stuck with one built-in game anymore."

Theo thought of his Roblox library, dozens of worlds all on one device. "It's like an app list," he said. "But you hold it in your hand."

Outside, a crowd had gathered around a different cabinet, where little green shapes marched slowly downward across the screen while a crowd of kids gasped.

"Space Invaders," the shopkeeper said. "Can't keep that one in stock."

Theo stepped up, grabbed the controls, and blasted a row of aliens just as they picked up speed. "They get faster the fewer there are," he said. "That's actually smart design."

"**1978**," Byte said. "Designer **Tomohiro Nishikado** made this for a company called Taito, and it kicks off a worldwide arcade craze. Arcades start running out of quarters to give as change."

"Out of *quarters*?" Theo laughed. "That's wild."

He slid the cartridge back into the console himself, clicking it into place like he'd done it a hundred times. "Okay. I get why this mattered."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Pizza, a Slump, and a Very Deep Hole (1980–1983)
chapters.text:
A man hunched over a drawing table, sketching a yellow circle with a wedge cut out of it.

"Is that supposed to be a mouth?" Theo asked.

"Close," the man said. "Toru Iwatani. I was eating dinner when I noticed a pizza with one slice gone. Thought — that's a face."

"Pac-Man," Theo said immediately. "Dude, that's such a random way to invent a character."

"That's the story, anyway," Byte said. "Nobody's one hundred percent sure the pizza part is exactly true, but Iwatani did create Pac-Man for Namco in **1980**, and it became one of the biggest games on Earth."

Theo took a turn chasing dots around a maze, ghosts trailing him, and gobbled a flashing power-up to turn the tables.

Then the scene shifted. Shelves that had been packed with games now sat half-empty, boxes piled by the register unsold.

"What happened here?" Theo asked.

"**1983**," Byte said. "So many rushed, low-quality games flooded stores that people stopped trusting any of them. Sales dropped hard — people call it the video game crash. Companies struggled. Some games never even made it off the shelf."

"That's kind of sad," Theo said.

"It gets a happier ending," Byte said, and the glow shifted them to a dusty desert lot where diggers worked a backhoe into dry ground.

"They're saying there's a huge pit out here full of busted cartridges," Byte said. "Games nobody could sell, including a famously bad E.T. game, buried in a New Mexico landfill — basically a giant trash pit."

"Is that even real?" Theo asked.

The backhoe scooped, and a cracked plastic cartridge tumbled out, label still readable.

"FOUND IT!" Theo shouted, pointing. "E.T.! That's actually real!"

"Diggers confirmed it in **2014**," Byte said, grinning. "Sometimes the wild stories check out."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Plumber Who Saved the Day (1985)
chapters.text:
The next room was lit up with a single TV showing a mustached man in overalls jumping over a gap.

A man with round glasses stood nearby, sketching the same character on paper. "Shigeru Miyamoto," he said. "I wanted a hero players would actually like. A plumber seemed friendly enough."

Theo grabbed the controller and lined up a jump. The plumber sailed over the gap, bonked a block overhead, and a coin popped out with a cheerful **DING**.

"Wait, you can hit blocks from underneath?" Theo asked, trying it again on purpose this time. Another coin popped free.

"Most people find that by accident too," Miyamoto said, smiling.

Theo spotted a pipe at the edge of the screen, slightly darker than the others. "That one's different. Bet it goes somewhere secret."

He dropped the plumber down it. The screen flashed, and a hidden room packed with coins appeared.

"Nice find," Miyamoto said, actually impressed.

"This is **1985**," Byte said. "**Nintendo** just launched the **NES** in the U.S., packaged with **Super Mario Bros.**, designed by Miyamoto right here. That console single-handedly brings the whole industry back from the crash you just saw."

Theo cleared the level, stomped a mushroom enemy flat, and grabbed a flag at the end of the course. "Mario's basically the most famous video game character ever, right?"

"Still is," Byte said. "Decades later."

Theo handed the controller back, a little reluctantly. "One more level?"

"There's always one more level," Byte said. "But we've got two more stops tonight."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Blocky World That Never Stops Growing (2011–Now)
chapters.text:
The portal's glow this time looked different — blocky, square-edged, almost exactly like his own game.

Theo stepped into a rolling green landscape made entirely of cubes: dirt, trees, even sheep, all built from squares. He laughed out loud. "This looks like Roblox's cousin."

"Close," Byte said. "This is **Minecraft**, released in **2011** by a Swedish developer named **Markus 'Notch' Persson**. It eventually became the best-selling video game of all time."

Theo punched a block of dirt, watched it pop loose, and stacked it into a wobbly little tower — the same instinct he used every night in Roblox Studio. "It's basically just building, but the whole game IS the building."

"That's why it never gets old," Byte agreed.

Theo placed one more block on top, steadying the tower with his palm, and it held.

The glow shifted one last time, into a bright museum hall lined with glass cases — old cartridges, control boxes, a plaque glowing under soft lights.

"**The World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Byte said. "Opened in **2015**, at a museum called The Strong, in Rochester, New York. Every game you played tonight has a case in here somewhere."

Theo walked past Tennis for Two's oscilloscope, Pong's wooden cabinet, Mario's cartridge, Pac-Man's yellow circle. "I played *all* of these," he said quietly. "Tonight. That's insane."

"Ready to go build your own level of history?" Byte asked.

The glow swallowed them both.

Theo landed back on his bed, blanket still tented over his head, laptop screen glowing its normal blue. His half-finished obby sat exactly where he'd left it — except now, tucked in the corner of the screen, one tiny green pixel blinked once, like a wink, before fading.

Theo grinned and pulled his blanket down. Downstairs, a ball sat by the back door, waiting for soccer practice tomorrow. Up here, a half-built jump pad waited too.

"Let's go live," he murmured, and finally closed the laptop.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, after soccer, he had a whole new level to build.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Rumbling Mountain
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip to the fire inside the Earth

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Juno lined up her dinosaurs on the rug. Milo stacked LEGO bricks into a little mountain. Theo sat close by, tablet dark, waiting for his turn.

Then Milo's mountain started to glow.

RUMMMBLE.

The little brick mountain shook. A puff of orange light popped out the top, like a tiny burp.

"Whoa!" said Juno, dropping her stegosaurus.

A tiny voice came from inside the bricks. "Hello! I'm Rumble. I'm a volcano."

Milo picked up the glowing brick carefully. "A volcano is a hole in the ground," he said slowly, remembering his book. "Hot stuff comes out."

"That's right!" said Rumble, bouncing happily. "A volcano is an opening where hot melted rock, ash, and gas sneak out from deep underground."

"Like a burp from the Earth!" said Juno, giggling.

"Exactly like a burp," said Rumble. "Want to see where the burps come from?"

Theo leaned forward. "Yes. Show us everything."

The glowing brick got brighter and brighter, until the whole bedroom filled with orange light, and the rug disappeared beneath them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Hot Soup Underground
chapters.text:
They landed on warm, rocky ground. Steam curled up around their feet.

"Where are we?" asked Milo, looking around.

"Inside my story," said Rumble. "This hot melted rock is called magma when it's under the ground. Once it comes out on top, we call it lava."

"Magma down low, lava up top," said Milo, testing the words.

Juno poked a toe near a little glowing crack. "Is it like dinosaur soup?"

"Kind of!" laughed Rumble. "Thick, hot, glowy soup, way under your feet."

Theo noticed a crack hissing with smoke. "Is that where it gets out?"

"Yes!" said Rumble. "Every volcano has an opening, like a chimney, for the hot soup and smoke to escape."

Milo tapped the crack gently with a stick. A tiny puff of steam popped out. POOF!

"It's like the Earth sneezing," Milo said.

"Gesundheit, Earth," said Theo, and Juno laughed so hard she snorted.

Rumble bounced. "Ready to see where volcanoes like to live?"

"Yes!" they all shouted together.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Horseshoe
chapters.text:
Rumble led them up into the sky, high above a big blue ocean.

"Look down," said Rumble. "See that ring of mountains around the edge?"

Theo squinted, the way he studied his soccer field before a game. He traced the shape with his finger. "It's shaped like a giant horseshoe!"

"Good eye!" said Rumble. "That's the Ring of Fire. It circles the Pacific Ocean, and most of the world's volcanoes live right along it."

"Why there?" asked Milo.

"The ground isn't one solid piece," said Rumble. "Earth's outside is cracked into giant puzzle pieces called plates. Volcanoes love to pop up where those plates push, pull, or slide past each other."

Juno frowned at the puzzle pieces below. "Like when my dinosaur puzzle gets wiggly?"

"Just like that," said Rumble.

"Which country has the most volcanoes?" asked Theo.

"Indonesia," said Rumble. "More than anywhere else on Earth."

Theo grinned. "That's basically the goalie of volcano countries. Busiest spot on the field."

Milo didn't totally get the joke, but he laughed anyway, and so did Juno, just to join in.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Hawaii's Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
They swooped down onto a green island, where a wide, round mountain rose gently from the ground.

"This is Kilauea," said Rumble. "It's one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. It has been bubbling and flowing for years and years."

"Why is it here, on an island, not at the edge of the puzzle pieces?" asked Theo.

"Good question," said Rumble. "Hawaii sits over a hotspot — one hot spot deep inside the Earth that stays still while the ground slides over the top of it."

Juno studied Kilauea's shape. "It's round like my stegosaurus's back. Not pointy."

"Smart noticing!" said Rumble. "Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, like this one. Others are tall and pointy, like a party hat."

Milo pulled out two LEGO bricks and built both shapes on the grass: one low and round, one tall and sharp.

"This one," he said, pointing to the wide model, "is probably stronger. More spread out."

"You'd make a good volcano builder," said Rumble. "There's an even bigger one nearby. Mauna Loa rises over four thousand meters above the sea. It's the biggest active volcano on Earth."

Theo whistled. "That's like stacking a thousand school buses."

Juno gasped. "I want to climb it!"

"Maybe when you're older," said Rumble, smiling. "For now, let's just admire it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Baby Island
chapters.text:
Rumble flew them north, over cold, gray water, to a spot near Iceland.

"Watch the water," said Rumble.

Bubbles popped. Steam hissed. Then, with a WHOOOSH, a chunk of black rock pushed up out of the waves.

"A new island!" shouted Milo.

"This really happened," said Rumble. "In 1963, an underwater volcano kept erupting and erupting, until a brand new island rose out of the sea. They named it Surtsey."

Juno's eyes went huge. "The ocean made a baby island?"

"The volcano did," said Rumble, smiling. "Iceland has lots of volcanoes, because it sits right where two giant puzzle pieces are slowly pulling apart."

Milo imagined his LEGO ocean set at home. "I'm building that when we get back. An island popping up out of blue bricks."

"I'll help," said Theo. "I'm good at the explosion sound effects."

He made a noise so loud that Juno covered her ears and laughed.

Rumble bounced along the new black rock. "Ready for somewhere even bigger? Somewhere not even on Earth?"

"WHAT?" said all three at once.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Mountain on Mars
chapters.text:
The light flashed red, then they were standing on dusty orange ground, looking up.

Way, way up.

"This is Olympus Mons," said Rumble. "It's a volcano on Mars. The biggest one we know of in the whole solar system."

Theo tipped his head back as far as it would go, and still couldn't see the top. "How big?"

"About thirteen miles tall," said Rumble. "Almost three times taller than Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on Earth."

Theo's mouth dropped open. "That's taller than anything in any game I've ever built."

"No soccer ball would ever come down from that," said Milo, and Theo cracked up.

Juno patted the orange dust. "Does a dinosaur live up there?"

"No dinosaurs on Mars," said Rumble gently. "It's much too cold and dusty for dinosaurs. But it's still pretty amazing, right?"

"Amazing," Juno agreed, nodding hard, kicking up little puffs of orange dust with her sneaker.

They all looked up at the enormous mountain together, three small astronauts under a giant orange sky.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Sleepy Giant
chapters.text:
Next, Rumble brought them to a wide, grassy valley with steam curling out of the ground.

"This is Yellowstone," said Rumble. "There's a huge, sleepy volcano hiding under here."

Juno froze. "Sleepy volcanoes wake up!"

"Not this one, not anytime soon," said Rumble kindly. "Scientists watch it very closely. Its last really big eruption was about six hundred forty thousand years ago. Right now, there's no sign it's waking up at all."

Juno let out a breath. "Phew."

"Grown-up scientists keep an eye on it every single day," said Rumble. "You can relax and enjoy the steamy pools."

Milo found a little bubbling pool and watched it pop. "It's just burping quietly," he said.

"Exactly," said Rumble. "A quiet burp, not a big one."

Theo grinned. "Good. I didn't bring my running shoes."

Juno giggled, already feeling better, and went back to watching the bubbles with Milo, poking at the warm steam with one careful finger.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Listening to the Ground
chapters.text:
"One more stop," said Rumble, "before bedtime."

They landed near a little hut with blinking lights and wiggly lines on a screen.

"This machine is a seismograph," said Rumble. "It feels tiny wobbles in the ground, way before we'd ever feel them ourselves."

Theo watched the wiggly line. "So it's like... listening for the Earth's heartbeat?"

"That's a perfect way to put it," said Rumble.

Milo noticed dark soil nearby, full of plants. "Why do so many plants grow right next to a volcano?"

"Ash from a volcano turns into fertile soil," said Rumble, "soil that's extra good for growing things. That's why farmers like living near volcanoes, even with the risk."

Juno patted the dark dirt. "Volcano dirt makes good flowers."

"It really does," said Rumble.

The orange light began to glow again, swirling around all three of them.

"Time to go home," said Rumble softly.

The light shrank, smaller and smaller, until —

They were back on the rug, in their own bedroom. Milo's LEGO brick mountain sat quiet and dark, just an ordinary brick again. But on top of it, one tiny new brick glowed the faintest orange, just for a second, like a wink.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Sleep tight, little volcanoes.
